title: Easton forfeits boys' game to Cambridge-SD
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Easton forfeits boys' game to Cambridge-SD

 January 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 721
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Easton High's boys' basketball team has forfeited its game Thursday at Cambridge-South Dorchester.Thursday's girls' game between the two schools will be played as scheduled at Easton High at 4 p.m., but spectators will not be allowed to attend.
The decision to forfeit the boys' game and play the girls' game without spectators is largely connected to the Oct. 27 football game between the two schools at Easton High that was stopped with just under 7 minutes remaining in the third quarter because of altercations away from the playing field.
At that game, the Easton and Cambridge-SD coaching staffs led their teams off the field while fans were instructed to leave the stadium by school administrators and local law enforcement officers. Three teenagers were arrested following the altercations.
The pattern that is emerging — basketball games scheduled between the two schools at Easton High this season will be played without fans; basketball games slated for Cambridge-SD will be forfeited by Easton High. The issue came down to playing the game with limited spectators. Easton wanted to limit or play without spectators. Cambridge-SD wanted spectators allowed.
This past Sunday, Easton High announced on its Instagram page, "Due to events that occurred during the EHS vs. CSD football game in the Fall, we have decided not to allow spectators at our upcoming girls and boys basketball game against CSD at Easton High School. As always, safety is a top priority. We apologize for any inconvenience and thank you for your support and understanding."
On Tuesday, the administrative offices of Cambridge-South Dorchester posted a statement on its Facebook page announcing Easton's decision to forfeit Thursday's boys' game at Cambridge-SD, and the Feb. 15 girls' game slated at Cambridge-SD.
"It is with great disappointment that we must convey this news: Easton High School has decided to forfeit the upcoming girls' and boys' basketball games scheduled to be held at Cambridge South Dorchester High School on Jan. 11 and Feb. 15," the statement said. "This decision was made by Easton High School and was not influenced by Cambridge-South Dorchester High in any way."
The post went on to say, "As a result of Easton High School's prearranged decision to forfeit these games, Cambridge South Dorchester High School will be credited with the wins for both of the boys' and girls' teams. We regret that parents, spectators and community members will not have the opportunity to witness these anticipated games.
"While we extend our best wishes to Easton High School, it is essential to emphasize that safety remains our top priority. We too understand the importance of maintaining a safe and secure environment for all involved.
Cambridge-SD High School was closed Wednesday due to weather conditions. Phone calls to the office of Cambridge-SD athletic director Casey O'Bier went unanswered.
On Wednesday, Talbot County Public Schools released a second statement in an email, saying that following the football game, administrators talked with coaches, athletes and parents about safety at future events.
"TCPS made the difficult decision not to allow spectators at upcoming home basketball events against CSD," the statement read.
Home games against Cambridge-SD will be livestreamed.
The statement continued that Talbot County school administrators asked that Cambridge-SD limit spectators at their home games.
"They chose not to," according to the Talbot County schools statement.
"Because the safety of our students and staff is always our highest priority, we have decided not to travel to CSD for the boys' and girls' basketball games on Jan. 11 and Feb. 15, thereby forfeiting those games," the statement read. "We value our relationship with our Dorchester County neighbors and believe this decision is in the best interests of all of the athletes involved."
The Easton and Cambridge-SD rivalry is one of the Bayside Conference's richest, especially in football and boys' basketball.
Entering Thursday's boys contest, Cambridge-SD (7-0 overall) was sitting atop the North Bayside with a 6-0 record and bidding for its first division title since 2020. Following the Vikings are second-place Queen Anne's (6-1) and Easton (5-1). Thursday's forfeit moves the Vikings to 8-0 overall and 7-0 in the division, while Easton slips to 6-4 overall, 5-2 division.
The boys' game at Easton is scheduled for Feb. 15 and will not have spectators.
Cambridge-SD's girls enter today's game at 5-2 overall, 4-2 North, trailing division leaders Queen Anne's (7-0, 6-0) and Kent Island (6-1, 6-0). Easton's girls are currently 3-6, 3-3.
Star Democrat Reporter Natalie Jones contributed to this article.

title: KINGS AND QUEENS
author: Bill Haufe
content:
KINGS AND QUEENS

 January 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1226
 Words 

 Read News Document

 SNOW HILL — It was a first for Cambridge-South Dorchester High's boys track program and head coach Clint Falduto.But it was the last conference indoor title run for Kent Island's girls team, at least under head coach Justin Holland.
Tori Willis Jr., won two individual titles to lead the Vikings to their first boys team crown indoors in school history, and Gabrielle Bernhard struck gold twice and set a new standard Wednesday, pacing the Buccaneers to their fifth girls title in six years during the Bayside Conference indoor track and field championships at the Worcester County Recreation Center.
"I was nervous," said Holland of the girls' competition, which ended with Kent Island totaling 96½ points — 23 ahead of runner-up Parkside.
Holland, who is set to retire from coaching after this season, had reason to be nervous.
Historically a power in the middle- and long-distance events, the Bucs did not score a point in the 1,600 or 3,200 meters Wednesday, had Kaitlyn Stevens place fifth for their only points in the 800, and were an uncharacteristic fifth in the 4x800 relay.
"This is not the stereotypical Kent Island track team," Holland said. "The four-by-eight (relay), I can't remember us not either winning, or you know, (placing) top three in the four-by-eight. I'm not used to this.
"And then when it comes to the (800), that's when we usually win the meet," Holland continued. "It's tight and then we go to the 800 and we triple score in the eight, and we seal the deal, because everybody knows we're going to be in the top four in the four-by-four relay. It was interesting."
Bernhard helped make up for those rare deficiencies, leading a 1-2-4 finish in both the 500 meters and pole vault.
"I'm happy that she switched over from cheerleading to track," Holland said of Bernhard, who did cheer and ran indoors last year, but is running track only this year.
Like many of Wednesday's competitors, Bernhard ran all her events in a fairly tight time frame. She placed second to Cambridge-SD's Enazajah Young (8.76 seconds) in the 55 hurdles, clocking a 9.03. She came right back and took fourth (45.26) in the 300. Two events later, she was back on the track, running the 500.
"Last year she was in the four-by-two (relay), but I had to drop her all the time because the four-by-two and the pole vault were all in the same (time) spot," Holland said. "So this year she's been scoring individually in the three and the five. And she wasn't a 500 runner. But she ran cross country this year so she knew she was in shape. So I said, 'Let's try the 500.' Of course that's the one she won."
But it took some doing, as she rallied past sophomore teammate Reece Heyliger over the final 50 meters to win in 1:24.59. Heyliger, who overcame a false start in the 55 to run strong legs for the second-place 4x200 relay and first-place 4x400 relay, was second in 1:24.78, followed by teammate Siena Koch (1:27.66) in fourth.
Bernhard, who early in the season broke Fiona Mulligan's school indoor pole vault record when she cleared 11 feet, 1 inch, capped her day by winning the pole vault with a new conference record effort of 11-2. The senior was followed by teammates Siena Koch (8 foot) in second and Nora Koch (6-6) in fourth.
Parkside (1:53.95) won the 4x200, but Kent Island's team of Kendra Coffey, Siena Koch, Heyliger and Seryna Stephan was second in 1:57.12. The Bucs punctuated the ninth girls indoor championship of Holland's career in the 4x400 relay, as Heyliger, Coffey, Stephan and Stevens won in 4:31.45.
The defending Class 1A state champion in the girls 55 meters, Cambridge-SD's Young held off Parkside's RaNiya Corbin (7.56) to win the conference crown in 7.45, before coming back to win the 55 hurdles in 8.76.
"Enazajah is a talent that's hard to match," Falduto said. "She's just incredibly athletic. We're trying to build her stamina up for some more different events other than the short ones. This could be a great opportunity for her future after high school. Just excited to see how she continues to control this season."
Falduto was excited to see what his boys team could do this season, and Wednesday the Vikings showed why, rolling to their first Bayside title indoors with 134½ points — 74 points ahead of runner-up Kent Island.
"They're stacked," Holland said of Cambridge-SD.
At the top of that stack is Willis, who started his day by winning the 55 meters in 6.576 — nipping Parkside's Nasir Bolden (6.578) — then leading a 1-2-3 Vikings sweep in the 55 hurdles. Willis took gold in 8.07 seconds followed by teammates Antonio Blueford (second, 8.121) and Jaydene Smith (third, 8.129).
"We've been training Tori to prepare for a day like this, knowing that come the state meet it would not be a similar type (of situation)," Falduto said in reference to the tight time schedule. "We knew coming into the Bayside meet and the competition we had, that he had a great opportunity to be a medalist in all four events."
A junior, Willis placed second in the 300 (37.10) to Snow Hill's Logan Hurney (36.88) before closing his day with a third-place in the 500 (1:13.71), completing a 34-point day.
Competing indoors for the first time, sophomore Majestic Jones gave Cambridge-SD an added boost, winning the high jump with a leap of 5-10.
Then there was Viking junior Tekai Drummond, who logged runner-up finishes in the 1,600 (4:55.50), 3,200 (10:49.39) and 800 (2:09.11), and ran a leg on the third-place 4x400 relay.
"Tekai has been probably the backbone of our team," Falduto said. "He was a sprinter last year, rarely did an 800 here or there, but as he's moved now to the mile, two mile. What he has done has really changed the dynamics of our team.
"We had a goal set on having a championship year," Faldutot said of his boys team. "Starting off the postseason with the indoor Bayside championship is a huge success for our team, and where they're at, and where they're heading. We had a goal set and we accomplished it for the boys. Everybody showed up in my opinion so I was very excited about that."
Queen Anne's County junior Ben Marks looks comfortable and in command en route to winning the boys 1,600 meters (4:51.13) and 800 (2:03.25).
"We didn't want him to run too hard," Queen Anne's head coach Natasha Dawson said of Marks, who's been focusing on the 1,600 this indoor season. "He hasn't run the 800 competitively this season. So we needed to make sure he got a good time so that sets him up for a good heat in regions."
Easton's Jed Smith led from start to finish in the boys 3,200. The senior began widening his lead with six laps remaining and won in 10:41.28. Smith joined Colin Smith, Jacob Camper and William Orndoff to give the Warriors victory in the boys 4x800 relay (8:49.39).
The Warriors got a second individual champion, as senior Sumayah Wilkins won the high jump, clearing the bar at 5 feet. Easton's Marvin Foster was second in the boys shot put (42-10½).
North Caroline junior Morgan Knott outdueled Snow Hill's Allie Suarezapecheche to win the girls 800 in 2:36.43. Knott also teamed with sophomores Seanna Rupp, Reece Bisesi and Linda Ridgell for victory in the 4x800 relay (10:49.95). Ridgell was runner-up in the 3,200 (12:46.96).

title: TIME TRIALS
author: Bill Haufe
content:
TIME TRIALS

 February 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1299
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Giuseppe Mellinger needed a late block.Tremaine Jackson needed an extra minute.
And Scottie Ford. Well, he needed more time than either one of them.
No matter the time frame, Jackson, Ford and Mellinger each finished with the same result Saturday night at Queen Anne's County High, winning their respective weight classes at the Class 2A-1A East Regional wrestling championships.
"He's been one of our elite wrestlers for three years now," Queen Anne's head coach David Stricker said of Jackson, who with his 5-3 overtime victory against Rising Sun's Xzavier Brown in the 126-pound final earned his 99th career win. "Tremaine, he's just so quick. And his power has really come along this year. When he gets in on a leg it's really hard to fend off."
Saturday's region final was the third time Jackson and Brown faced off this season. Brown pieced together an 8-3 decision at the Westminster Duals in late December, then earned a 3-1 overtime win when the two met in the 2A-1A East Regional Duals earlier this month. Their third encounter would also take longer than six minutes.
"They've been wrestling each other since youth, so they've known each other really well," Stricker said. "I'm not surprised it went that far."
A senior, Jackson (35-3) scored a first-period takedown, but Brown escaped with 44 seconds left in the period to make it 2-1 after one. Brown (35-8) rode Jackson through a scoreless second period, and hit a reversal 11 seconds into the third period for a 3-2 lead. Jackson then got an escape off a restart with 15 seconds left in the third to forge a 3-3 tie, sending the match into a 1-minute overtime.
"It's obviously been a bit harder because they've been training him, trying to study my style, his coaches," Jackson said. "They obviously know me very well, the good moves I do. So yeah, it definitely was a lot more difficult than the other times wrestling him."
Brown got in a single-leg shot in the overtime, but Jackson blocked, spun and earned the takedown for the 5-3 sudden victory.
"My last match at the high school, and what was going through my head was, I can't lose," said Jackson, whose second regional title came five days after winning his third Bayside Conference crown. "I feel great. I put in the work. I think I've got a good shot of getting in the state finals."
Ford also had a familiar opponent in his 138-pound final — Parkside junior Rocco Tully — who the Kent County sophomore decisioned 6-0 in the Bayside championship five days earlier.
"I knew it was going to be tougher," said Ford, who coupled two takedowns with a reversal for Monday's 6-0 victory. "Every time you wrestle somebody it feels like it gets tougher and tougher. They always learn from it. I was nervous. I would have much rather faced somebody else I hadn't seen before."
After a scoreless first period, Ford (37-1) hit a switch off bottom for a reversal with 35 seconds left in the second period for a 2-0 lead. Tully (35-9) scored a takedown with 44 seconds to go in the third and rode Ford the rest of the period, forcing overtime.
Neither wrestler scored in the 1-minute overtime. Starting on top, Ford rode Tully through the first 30-second sudden-victory period. Less than two seconds into the second 30-second period, Ford reversed Tully and rode out the remainder of the period on top for the 4-2 win.
"I knew I had a good switch on him because on Monday I had a nice switch," Ford said. "He knows how to throw legs, so he's really tough on top, but I knew I could get out. I just beat him off the whistle."
Something that did not surprise Kent County head coach Chris Yiannakis.
"He's been on that switch," Yiannakis said of Ford. "That's one of his number one escapes from bottom. Most people can't stop it. It's so fast. Rocco did stop it in the first couple of periods though. He just wore him down by the final (period) and he couldn't stop it."
The 175-pound final was yet another Bayside rematch, as Mellinger (36-5) clashed with Parkside's Canaan Mapp (24-8) for the third time this season.
"The first time we wrestled he actually was more aggressive," said Mellinger, who defeated Mapp via a 12-4 major decision during the dual-meet season. "He would actually tie up with me and stuff. So that allowed me to work my offense. The second time, at Baysides (a 7-2 Mellinger win), he would run around, he kept moving, but I got a few takedowns there.
"This time, because I think his coaches were telling him how to make some good adjustments, he wasn't tying up," Mellinger continued. "He was keeping me at a distance. He would try to work in some shots, I would try to work in mine. But we both got a good shot defense. And then when we're so far apart, it's hard to score points."
Mellinger got a double-leg takedown 54 seconds into the match, but Mapp escaped 11 seconds later, making it 2-1 heading into the second. Mapp escaped five seconds into he second period to tie the match.
It remained that way until 18 seconds into the third, when Mellinger, starting on bottom, escaped to take a 3-2 lead. Mellinger blocked a shot midway through the period before a neutral restart with 41 seconds left. Mellinger got in a shot, but Mapp countered with a shot with less than 20 seconds left. The Kent Island senior, who was named the Bayside Conference's defensive player of the year in football for 2023, could not be taken down though, hanging on for the 3-2 win.
"I started getting a little nervous at the end when I took a shot and then he re-shot and got in on my leg with like 15 seconds left," Mellinger said. "And I was able to defend that because if he had gotten that and I didn't get up in time, that would have been the match."
It was Mellinger's first regional title.
"It's nice to win, said Mellinger, whose younger sister Lilliana won the 120-pound title at Friday night's girls 2A-1A East Regional. "My sister and I, we're both Bayside champions. Now, we're both regional champions. Now, we're both competing for a state title. That's cool. It's a lot of fun."
Said Kent Island head coach Tommy Sitar of Mellinger, "He had another great tournament. He worked really well in his matches leading up to the final, and fortunately got the win in the final. It's hard to beat a wrestler three times in a season. It's a good feat."
Kent Island seniors Greg Couch (132) and Cody Sandefer (144) each took runner-up honors, and seniors Brandon Adler (157) and Nick Morey (190) each won their consolation final to place third.
The top four in each weight class advance to this year's state tournament, which begins Thursday at the Show Place Arena in Upper Marlboro and concludes Saturday.
Stephen Decatur and Rising Sun each advanced nine to states, while North Caroline finished with the most wrestlers from a North Bayside school, qualifying six and two alternates.
"We had a rough Monday at Baysides," North Caroline head coach Robin Eaton said. "I preached to them all week 'That wasn't the week to shine. 'Work harder and fix a few things and we could shine at regionals.' And that's what they did. They did everything we worked on; wrestled very smart, wrestled tough. Didn't make mistakes."
North Caroline freshman Caleb Melvin (120), junior Corey Bunce (165) and senior Dakota Kinsey (285) each wrestled-back to win their respective consolation finals, while sophomores Darly Ortega (106), Connor Frank (113), and Jacob Carpenter (126) placed fourth.
Kent County senior Brady Sutton decisioned Harford Vo Tech's Nikolai Chervak in the 144-pound consolation final, and Cambridge-South Dorchester sophomore Mark Jones placed fourth at 285.

"We have obtained and are currently reviewing video surveillance footage as part of our ongoing efforts," the release stated. "No arrests have been made at this time as we continue to review evidence and fully investigate this incident."
Carver was winning 42-15 at halftime and extended that lead to 47-15, when Dorrian Sands hit a baseline jumper and a 3-pointer in the first minute.

title: CLOSING STATEMENTS
author: Bill Haufe
content:
CLOSING STATEMENTS

 March 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports

 UPPER MARLBORO — Giuseppe Mellinger didn't storm past his coaches, chuck his headgear in a fury, or try to leave an impression on the nearest concrete wall with his fist.The opportunity to direct blame was certainly there, but the Kent Island High senior refused to point a finger.
"I'm not going to make excuses for myself," Mellinger said in the wake of a 3-2 ultimate-tiebreaker loss in the 175-pound final during the Class 2A/1A state wrestling championship tournament at the Show Place Arena on March 2. "You try not to let refs dictate your match. Wrestling you know, you've got to be accountable. It's only you out there wrestling somebody else."
Of the 16 wrestlers from North Bayside schools that qualified for states, Mellinger was the only one to reach the finals in the boys competition.
"Coming from Kent Island, we rarely have people that make it that far," said Mellinger, who became just the third Buccaneer to reach the finals during Tommy Sitar's eight seasons as head coach — joining Matt Miller (2020) and Justin Thomas (2016). "So it was surreal to be there in that moment.
"Senior year. You've wrestled three years of high school," Mellinger added. "Wrestled since you were like five or six years old, and then you make it to the state finals. Like wow. This is it. But I felt pretty confident. I felt relaxed. That was my last match ever so I'm going to go out there and let it fly. Like it's just one more match."
On the way to that last match, Mellinger had earned a first-round 15-13 win over Hammond's Jaden Timithy in the first sudden-victory period, took a forfeit in the quarterfinals, then defeated Middletown senior Kashton Dalhouse (47-4) via a 5-4 decision in the semifinals.
That set up his title shot with South Carroll sophomore Anthony Rodrigues (47-3). With 45 seconds remaining in the first period, the lead official held up two fingers, signaling a two-point takedown for Mellinger. But that initial call was waved off when the official ruled Mellinger did not to have enough control.
"I thought I did too," said Mellinger when asked if he thought he had the takedown. "I didn't hear anybody argue against it. And the South Carroll guys, their body language was like, 'Yeah, wow. We got saved on that one.'"
Though he did not protest or go to the scorer's table for an explanation, Sitar also thought Mellinger had a takedown.
"I would have liked to see that call stand at two," Sitar said. "It wasn't something where they came to the table an overturned it or anything like that, or even that the second ref came in and overturned it."
It remained scoreless through the remainder of the first. Starting on bottom, Rodrigues scored an escape just two seconds into the second period for a 1-0 lead. Sixteen seconds into the third, Mellinger escaped off bottom, to make it 1-1. Mellinger blocked a shot 14 seconds later and after two restarts, the score remained 1-1 heading into overtime.
Mellinger got two deep shots in during the 1-minute overtime, but Rodrigues wouldn't be taken down as the duel moved into the two 30-second ride-out periods. Rodrigues again escaped with only two seconds elapsed for a 2-1 lead. Mellinger answered with an escape with six seconds left in the second ride-out, forging a 2-2 deadlock heading into the ultimate tiebreaker.
Because he had scored the match's first point, Rodrigues got to choose top or bottom to start the final period. Rodrigues took bottom and six seconds into the final stage pulled his left leg from Mellinger's grasp for a 3-2 victory.
"That (takedown) would have won the championship," said Sitar (39-6), who was bidding to become Kent Island's first state champion since 2015 when Stevan Smith won his second straight state title. "Whoever had a takedown was going to win because shots were so hard.
"I was hoping for a state title," Mellinger added. "But at the end of the day I was the aggressive wrestler. As the match went on, offense got harder and harder, especially when we got sweaty. Nothing you can down now."
Kent Island senior Greg Couch (132 pounds) had his hopes for a state championship end in Friday's semifinal round, when he lost a 12-6 decision to defending — and eventual — state champion JoJo Gigliotti of South Carroll.
"I think he gave him his toughest match," Sitar said of Couch's battle with Gigliotti. "I think he knew he had a match with Couch. I think had Couch been on the other side of the bracket I might have had a couple of finalists. Greg wrestled his butt off. He was peaking at the right time."
Couch looked headed for the consolation bracket, when he fell behind 4-0 in the first period of his opening match to Southern Garrett's Hayden Harvey.
"He got taken down twice and then it was like the switch was flipped," Sitar said of Couch. "He was ready to go. He was comfortable and he just let the rest of the weight class have it from there."
Starting with Harvey, who would not score another point while Couch was rallying for a 13-4 major decision. Couch earned a 7-1 decision over Huntingtown senior Jett Cramer (24-5) in the quarterfinals but then lost 12-6 to Gigliotti (51-1), who pinned his other three opponents in the tournament en route to his second state title.
"When I got into the consi round I realized, 'This is all or nothing,'" Couch said. "'This is my senior year. This is all I got left.'"
And it took some doing.
Couch and C. Milton Wright's Mitchell Nguyen (36-8) were tied 2-2 through regulation and overtime. Couch then rode Nguyen out through the first ride-out stage before working an escape in the second ride-out for a 3-2 win.
"That was definitely one of my hardest matches of the year, it not the hardest," Couch said of his bout with Nguyen.
In the consolation final, Couch crafted a 7-2 victory over Northern Garrett's Mason Glotfelty (39-5) for his 100th career victory and a third-place finish.
"I had a lot going through my mind before that last match," said Couch, who finished 33-9. "I had the support of my family. My dad and my uncle were on the mat coaching for me in my corner. It definitely provided me with everything I needed for that last match.
"It was definitely a hard path back to try to get third," Couch said. "They say second place usually looks the most upset and third is smiling a lot more, and I can definitely agree with that. Definitely makes a difference ending it on a win rather than a loss."
Queen Anne's County senior Tremaine Jackson earned his 100th career win when he earned a 54-second fall in his first-round match on Thursday, but watched his state-title aspirations end Friday with a 4-2 loss to Northern Garrett's Devon Opel (38-7) in the 126-pound quarterfinals.
"I had the whole night (Friday) to think about what happened," Jackson said of his loss. "I mean it hurt, but I knew I just had to bounce back, just start doing what I do best."
Jackson's road to the consolation final started Saturday morning with a 15-0 technical fall over Liberty's Alex Pearl in 3:15. He advanced to the consolation semifinals with a forfeit, then put together a 13-0 major decision over Eastern Vo Tech's Chase Ullman."
"The tech fall, the (Pearl) kid walked off the mat and he was like, 'Man, that kid is fricking good,' when he shook my hand," Queen Anne's head coach David Stricker said. "We were like, 'Yeah, we know.'
"He could just stop putting the pressure on himself and just go be Tremaine, and pretty much show off his full talents; his full arsenal," Stricker said of Jackson after his quarterfinal loss. "When he's there and he can just let it fly, there's not a whole lot of people that can stop him."
That included Rising Sun's Xzavier Brown, who faced off for a fourth time this season against Jackson in the consolation final and lost 5-2.
"It was close but I feel like I calculated that match," said Jackson, whose second consecutive third-place finish at states capped a 40-4 season. "I wrestled him a bunch of times. And that was my last high school match, so I was coming out on top regardless."

 DENTON — Rain didn't stop the approximately 45 runners and walkers who came out to support efforts to supply clean water in rural Ghana and Tanzania at the 14th Annual Walk for the "WELL" of it 5k Saturday morning in Denton.The race was organized by local nonprofit Lifetime Wells International and held at Lifetime Well Drilling off MD Route 404. The nonprofit has raised around $25,600, with donations still coming in.
Those who braved the wet, windy and chilly day ran laps around a track on the property.

Seek, Saints outduel Palmer, Lions

 ST. MICHAELS — Like many a game that shapes a division race, it was close.Each team turned an inning-ending double play.
Each team had a batter hit by a pitch and another intentionally walk.
Each team got outstanding performances from their big-name pitchers.
And each team finished with five hits.
But it was St. Michaels High's baseball team that produced the decisive — and what proved to be the last — hit. That hit came with two outs and the bases loaded in the bottom of the fifth inning Monday, when Jack Brennen chopped a slow bouncer down the third-base line for an infield hit that scored Pearson Greenwood with the winning run in a 3-2 Saints victory at Harold Baines Field.
St. Michaels (12-0 overall, 5-0 North Bayside) entered Tuesday tied atop the division with Colonel Richardson (12-1, 5-0) while Queen Anne's slipped to 9-3, 2-2.
"It was a very good high school baseball game," St. Michaels head coach Brian Femi said. "Both teams played well. It was an outstanding pitching duel. Both teams got timely hits. Both played good defense."
And both had scored two runs apiece heading into the bottom of the fifth.
That's when Will Sherwood lined a one-out single to center field. Queen Anne's right-hander Noah Palmer (3-1) walked Greenwood. Both runners advanced on a wild pitch before Palmer issued an intentional pass to Jacob Bealefeld, loading the bases. Henry Mullikin grounded to third baseman Jacob Clough, who threw home to force Sherwood at the plate for the second out.
Brennen then beat a grounder down the third-base line. Clough got to the ball, but didn't have time to make a throw to first as Greenwood raced home with the go-ahead run. Femi and Queen Anne's head coach Chris Fitzgerald agreed Brennen's bouncer was an infield hit — the last hit for either team the rest of the game.
"Heavyweight game for sure," Fitzgerald said. "They got the hit they needed and came away with the W."
Both pitchers were impressive, with St. Michaels senior left-hander Jacob Seek (4-0) striking out a season-high 13 in a complete-game victory. Seek allowed one earned run and walked two.
"This is what he's done all year," Femi said of Seek. "He just goes out and makes big pitches in big situations. The bigger the situation the bigger the pitcher. And he's a leader."
Queen Anne's Dalton Brown led off the game with a single, but Seek struck out the next three batters.
Down 2-0, the Lions had a rally working in the second, when Clough walked on four pitches and Colin Siwald singled to left. Seek fanned Bobby McCarthy, but Palmer reached with a bunt single up the third-base line, loading the bases. Gavin Leith grounded into a fielder's choice that plated Clough to make it 2-1. Seek ended the inning when Brown skied out to center.
"At moments it was little tight, but I think we did a good job of pulling out of it and being efficient," Seek said. "My curveball was on point today I felt like. I felt like I had a little mechanical issue that I had to (work the) kink out early. And I think when I figured that out in that second inning it kind of picked up for me and I was able to be more efficient with my pitches and hit my locations."
The Lions though pulled even in the top of the third. With one out, Seek struck out Dulin Clark. But the ball kicked away from Mullikin behind the plate. By the time St. Michaels' catcher located and retrieved the ball over by the St. Michaels dugout, Clark was on second. Evan Dickey then laced a 1-2 offering up the middle to score Clark with the tying run.
The closest Queen Anne's came to breaking the 2-2 tie was in the fourth. Leith reached on an infield hit and moved to second on a passed ball. After Brown was intentionally walk, Seek fanned Noah Cramer to end the inning.
Seek retired nine of the final 10 batters he faced. McCarthy reached with one out in the sixth when he was hit by a pitch before Palmer bounced to Bealefeld at third to a 5-4-3 inning-ending double play.
"That turned the game around I thought," Femi said. "Jake's played well for us all year. And that just swung the momentum our way."
Palmer delivered yet another quality performance for the Lions, striking out eight and walking four in 5 1/3 innings.
"I thought he was fantastic," Femi said of Palmer. "He beat us last year. We haven't hit him in two years. He competes. He changes speeds. He throws multiple pitches. I think he's one of the better pitchers in the Bayside."
But the Saints pushed two runs across in the home half of the first. Connor Wheeler was hit by a pitch and stole second base. Sherwood reached on an error, advancing Wheeler to third. Palmer looked like he might escape any damage when he struck out Greenwood and Bealefeld. But Mullikin drove a 1-1 pitch up the middle to score Wheeler and Sherwood for a 2-0 lead. Brennen followed with a single before Palmer fanned Bobby Fink to end the frame.
"After that first inning, it was rough," Palmer said. "But I came back and I feel like I was dialed in."
Blending his fastball and curve, Palmer wouldn't face more than four batters over the next three innings. Wheeler hit a two-out single in the second, stole second base and moved to third on a passed ball before Palmer got Sherwood to bounce out to third. The right-hander walked Bealefeld with one out in the third. Mullikin flew out to center fielder Brown, who fired a strike to first to double off Bealefield for the inning-ending double play.
Brock Grow got on via a two-out walk in the fourth and advanced to second on a passed ball. But Palmer got a called third strike on Ethan Royer to strand Grow. St. Michaels stranded seven baserunners, six in scoring position.
"He hasn't had a bad game," Fitzgerald said of Palmer. "We've put him up against all the big teams we got to go up against and we're proud the way he's handled himself all year. This wasn't surprising. Every game he's always performed like he did today. Just a stud for us. Proved it again today. Wish we could have gotten a couple more hits for him here and there and the game might have turned out different. But he did everything we asked of him today."
Palmer struck out Grow to open the sixth before reaching his pitch limit and being relieved by Brown, who struck out both batters he faced.
Queen Anne's stranded six, two in scoring position.
NORTH DORCHESTER 14 CAMBRIDGE-SD 4
SHILOH — Manny Reyes hit an RBI triple and Blake Bramble smacked a game-ending two-run triple in the sixth to lead the Eagles (6-5).
John Boyle earned the win, giving up three hits and striking out six in three innings. Brock Warrell threw three innings of relief.

Montana Davis had two hits and two RBIs for the Colonels (9-4) and Kylie Rhinehardt had two hits and one RBI. Sadie Prettyman added two hits, and Eileen Johnson (two RBIs), Kendall Sann (RBI) and Clarissa Peugh (RBI) had one hit apiece.

 EASTON — Saints Peter and Paul High girls head lacrosse coach Alison Beyer knew her team wasn't playing to its potential.So did sophomore standout Caroline Ewing.
"After the first quarter, Caroline, I could see it in her eyes. She let the team have it," Beyer said. "Normally I give my spiel. And she said you guys better straighten up. "Obviously, we never play to not win," Beyer said after the Sabres won their 13th straight game. "But for whatever reason I think we took today for granted. And Caroline never does not play to her full potential. She has matured so much this season both mentally and skillfully."
Emily Currie (team-high five goals) converted passes from Dakota Lhotsky and Miranda Stup to give Easton (6-4) and 2-0 lead before the game was 2 minutes old.
It appeared the Warriors made it 3-0 moments later, but officials waved off the goal. Ewing gained possession and went from end to end before scoring to make it 2-1. Easton's Anna Crist notched the first of her two goals to restore the home team's two-goal lead. Ewing answered just 8 seconds later to make it a one-goal deficit again.
Back-to-back goals from Lhotsky — the second off a Currie feed — pushed the Warrior lead to 5-2 with 2:19 left in the opening quarter.
"We came out ready to play," said Easton head coach Katie Lowman, who got a monster performance from goalie Zelia Proa. "I could not have asked them to do anything more. Saints Peter and Paul is incredibly talented. Most people probably didn't expect the score to be that close."
Ewing again responded, scoring twice in a 31-second window to pull Sts. Peter & Paul within 5-4 at the end of the first quarter.
"She really took control of today's game," Beyer said of Ewing.
Easton was far from finished.
Stup set up another Currie goal to make it 6-4 with 16 seconds elapsed in the second quarter.
Ewing scored her fifth goal, then set up Morgan Quade's first to forge a 6-all tie with 8:05 left in the second. A little over a minute later, Emery Zimmerman gave the Sabres (13-1) their first lead at 7-6. Easton's Addie Knox (three goals) scored to create the game's second tie.
But Ewing scored her sixth goal before Eden Zimmerman and Emery Zimmerman each converted free-position chances for a 10-7 Sabres lead with 1:32 to go in the first half.
Kylie Kroniser then drew a yellow card for incidently hitting an Easton player in the head while attempting a clear. Knox and Currie scored in the final minute of the first half to get the Warriors within 10-9. Myka Motovidlak then tied the game 50 seconds into the third quarter.
Emery Zimmerman nudged the Sabres back in front. Stup set up Currie's final goal to tie the game for a fourth time at 11-11.
Again Ewing took charge, setting up goals by Eden Zimmerman and Quade just 34 seconds apart for a lead the Sabres never surrendered at 13-11. Quade completed her hat trick with just under 2 minutes left in the third to make it 14-11.
"The dynamic of her and Quade has been something," Beyer said of Ewing and her senior star, who on Wednesday went over 200 goals and 400 points for her high school career. "I wish there was more time for those two to play together. The relationship of their play has been something to see. And it really showed today more than any past games."
Easton put together one last flurry, Crist scoring with 4:38 left, and Knox making it 14-13 with 1:59 left. Currie then earned a free-position chance with under a minute left and fired a low shot that Kylie Kroniser stopped with her foot. Kendall Kroniser gained position, eluded two Warriors, then raced down the sideline as the Sabres drained the remaining clock.
"I was so nervous," Kylie Kroniser said. "I was very stressed but I just kept calm. I kept my cool. I wasn't emotional about it like last year. But the foot save was the best."
While Beyer said the Kronisers helped "save the day", she also praised the play of Proa, who stoped a slew of close-range shots to keep the Warriors in the game from start to finish.
"Their goalie was on fire," Beyer said. "She was phenomenal."

title: Maryland horse racing has peaks and valleys through the decades
author: Ted Black tblack@somdnews.com
content:
Maryland horse racing has peaks and valleys through the decades

 May 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ted Black tblack@somdnews.com | Section: State News 
 
 1645
 Words 

 Read News Document

 While many horse racing enthusiasts often associate racing in Maryland with the upcoming Preakness Stakes, the famed middle jewel in thoroughbred racing's Triple Crown for three-year-olds, the Free State actually offers racing virtually year round for both thoroughbred and standardbred horses, both of which have plenty of common synergies.Both thoroughbred and standardbred racing in Maryland can trace their roots through a handful of families that have a continued impact on the "Sport of Kings" at thoroughbred tracks Laurel Park, Pimlico Race Course and Timonium Race Track, as well as harness racing venues Rosecroft Raceway and Ocean Downs. Timonium hosts seven days of live racing each summer in conjunction with the Maryland State Fair.
Throughout the decades several Maryland tracks have come and gone, including two thoroughbred tracks located in Prince George's County — Bowie and Marlboro — as well as in Havre de Grace, a former track in Harford County that got a mention in the 1973 film "The Sting," which centered around gambling and horse racing. Bowie operated from 1914-1985 as a race track, then remained open as a training center until 2014 when all the horses were relocated to Laurel, Pimlico or Fair Hill, a training center in Cecil County.
Thoroughbred trainers Dale Capuano and Gary Capuano have been recognizable figures in Maryland racing for over four decades. Dale Capuano retired from training at the end of 2022 with 3,662 winners who earned over $68 million from 18,686 starts topped by Grade II winner and millionaire Heros Reward. Gary Capuano, who has already conditioned a pair of millionaires, Cherokee's Boy and Captain Bodgit, both of which were Preakness Stakes participants, still trains horses on the circuit and could have another Preakness starter on May 18 in Copper Tax.
A sophomore son of Copper Bullet that Capuano trains for Rose Petal Stable LLC, Copper Tax recently overcame a stumbled start to rally from well off the pace to capture the $125,000 Federico Tesio Stakes at Laurel Park. Considered Maryland's last local prep for its most famous race, Copper Tax punched his ticket to the 149th Preakness Stakes with his determined score in the Federico Tesio by getting the one mile and one-eighth distance in 1:52.01.
"I was hoping, you know, that we had a chance after that troubled beginning," Capuano said. "Of course, I was watching Ness's horse [Speedyness] on the lead and I'm like, nobody's going with him and that's not good [for my horse]. But he just kept sustaining that run. We'll see [about the Preakness]. We'll see how he comes out. And, you know, like I said before, he's not a big horse."
Thoroughbred trainer Linda Gaudet and her daughter Lacey Gaudet were both fixtures on the Bowie backstretch before it closed for training purposes in 2014, as was longtime horseman Eddie Gaudet, Linda's husband and Lacey's father, who passed away in 2018 at the age of 87, six years after he had retired from training to turn the operation over to his wife and daughter.
During his career, Eddie Gaudet enjoyed ample success with stakes horses as well as claimers, with Marry Me Do, Winning Point, Star Touch and Concealed Identity among his top trainees. Like Copper Tax, Concealed Identity punched his ticket to the Preakness Stakes at age 3 by taking the Tesio Stakes — run at Pimlico that year — his only entrant in the middle jewel of racing's triple crown.
An annual revivalThoroughbred racing has fallen well below the public radar over the last two decades, although its interest gets revived each spring with the famed Triple Crown series — the Kentucky Derby at Churchill Downs on May 4, the Preakness Stakes at Pimlico on May 18 and the Belmont Stakes at Belmont Park on June 8.
But even interest in the Belmont Stakes is often contingent on whether or not one horse is still in contention to sweep all three legs after both the Derby and Preakness have been contested.
Speaking of the Triple Crown, while there have been 13 horses that completed the coveted sweep, perhaps no horse is more synonymous with the three events than Secretariat. Voted horse of the year at age 2 and again at age 3, Secretariat actually owns the track record for all three Triple Crown races, winning the one mile and one-quarter Derby in 1:59.2, the one mile and three-sixteenths Preakness in 1:53 and the one mile and one-half Belmont in 2:24.
Maryland lawmakers recently promoted House Bill 1524, which would shift ownership of the two thoroughbred tracks from the Stronach Family to the state, and Pimlico is expected to get a $400 million facelift. During its renovation, the Preakness Stakes will be contested at Laurel Park, then after the renovations at Pimlico are completed in 2026 Laurel Park would permanently close for live racing and be sold to developers.
Pimlico would remain as the lone track with meets centered around the Preakness Stakes in the spring and Maryland Million Day in the fall.
Horsing around historyMarlboro Race Track, currently the site of the Prince George's Equestrian Center and Show Place Arena, had a brief, bizarre history. Marlboro offered live racing three weeks each summer from 1914-1973. After it closed, the grandstand burned down in 1980 and live racing returned there two days each fall from 1988-1993, but it has not offered live racing in over 30 years since.
Standardbred driver Jonathan Roberts, a 1999 St. Mary's Ryken High School graduate and perennial leading driver at Rosecroft Raceway with nearly 4,700 driving victories in a career that began shortly after he graduated from high school, is part of a family that also has deep ties to the sport. His father, trainer William "Bib" Roberts, began racing horses at Rosecroft over 50 years ago when the oval was one-half mile in circumference.
"When I was a kid, I really didn't have much interest in the horses," the younger Roberts recalled. "I always liked racing motorcycles and dirt bikes. I really wasn't into the horses. It really wasn't until I got into high school that I started going to the track more and helping my dad train horses. I think I knew from the first time that I climbed into the bike to jog a horse that I knew that driving horses was for me."
Jonathan Roberts attained his racing license soon after graduating from St. Mary's Ryken and he has never looked back. Among the perennial dash-winning drivers at Rosecroft the past 15 years, he has primarily enjoyed success with horses trained by his father, including Great George Two, Rocktavius, Capital Builder and Starship, along with others trained by his sister, Megan Roberts, another St. Mary's Ryken alum, including HP Lis Shadow.
But Jonathan Roberts also boosts numerous wins for perennial leading trainer Mike Hall, including Can't Beach That, a two-time horse of the meet at Rosecroft.
"Early on I pretty much only drove for my dad, but when other opportunities came along I had to take them," Roberts said. "Sometimes I have to choose between one of my dad's or one of Megan's and one of Mike Hall's and I typically drive the one that I think has the best chance of winning on that night. It's never an easy decision, but I think everyone understands what goes into it."
Like Roberts, trainer-driver Russell Foster also hails from a harness racing family that has deep roots in the sport. Unlike Roberts, whose initial interest in the sport was secondary, Foster has known since elementary school that he was destined to earn his living training and driving standardbreds. Like Roberts, Foster is also among the perennial driving leaders at Rosecroft and Ocean Downs.
"I basically knew from the time I was like 7, 8 years old that I was going to train horses," said Foster, who eclipsed the 2,000-win plateau in his driving career one year ago. "Then once I started working in the paddock, I knew that was going to be my life. I started out training horses, but then about 10 years ago I started driving some of my own and when I started winning with Hi Sir, that kind of put me on the map."
Running at RosecroftRosecroft Raceway, which offers live harness two nights each week during the spring and again in the fall for a total of 60 days, typically conducts live racing on Tuesday and Thursday evenings. But the harness track will look to piggyback on the popularity of the Triple Crown races by offering live cards on Saturday, May 4, and again on Saturday, May 18, to correspond with the Derby and Preakness.
Rosecroft, which opened in 1949, was initially a half-mile racing oval owned by William E. Miller and remained in his family for nearly 40 years before being sold to real estate mogul Mark Vogel, who reconfigured the racing surface from one-half-mile to its current five-eighths mile status in 1989. Pacer Forrest Skipper (1:54) and trotter Mack Lobell (1:56) were the all-age track records on the former half-mile surface.
Since being reconfigured to a five-eighths mile oval, Rosecroft has witnessed its fair share of world record holders among pacers and trotters, including Hi Lan Tye, Nuclear Breeze and Allywag Hanover on the pacing side and Vivid Photo on the trotting side.
Allywag Hanover lowered the track and world record to 1:46.4 with his victory in the 2022 edition of the $125,000 Potomac Stakes, although the world record has since been eclipsed at a different five-eighths mile oval.
When Rosecroft is dark for live racing, Ocean Downs, a half-mile oval in Berlin, five miles west of Ocean City, fills the void for owners, trainers, drivers and fans. Ocean Downs offers live racing 44 nights each summer with this year's meet slated to commence on May 31 and run through September 5.
Like Rosecroft, Ocean Downs hosts Maryland Sire Stakes events for two- and three-year-old pacers and trotters each summer.
Wherever horse racing may be headed in Maryland, it's history is cemented in a number of historic tracks.

title: SOARING TO GOLD
author: Bill Haufe
content:
SOARING TO GOLD

 July 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1048
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Aliah Raga has spent a lot of time airborne.She has worked on takeoffs and landings.
She has built speed then soared upwards as if ready to pierce the roof over her head. She has altered those trajectories with suddenness and grace, commanding her 5-foot frame into streamline flips and twists that are a mix between Simone Biles and Peter Pan.
She has come down only to go right back up, launching into a second high-flying, acrobatic arc that preferably ends with both feet planted firmly in one place, as she raises her arms and breaks into a glamorous smile.
Aliah Raga has spent a lot of time honing, polishing and perfecting the components of the double mini trampoline.
A lot of time.
"I've been doing the sport for 11 years," said Raga, formerly of Denton. "It took a lot of practices. A lot of hard days. And a lot of falling."
So when 19-year-old Raga and her United States trampoline and tumbling teammates received late notification about a schedule change on Day 1 of the FIG World Cup in Coimbra, Portugal on July 6, they were left little time to stretch, warm up and mentally prepare prior to their first pass.
Raga was angry.
And that has often proved not to be a good thing for the competition.
"I was actually really angry," Raga said during a phone interview last week. "And for some reason, I don't know why, but I seem to do well when I'm angry, or I feel I have something to prove."
Raga harnessed her anger enough to get through that first day, then came back the following day to post the competition's highest score en route to winning the gold medal in the women's double mini trampoline for her first international championship.
"Definitely," Raga said when asked if she surprised herself. "Honestly, I was just going to land two passes, have fun, and try my best to represent my country."
Fun.
Raga has had a lot of fun since beginning her gymnastics journey at Joan Dyott's Chesapeake Gymnastics in Easton when she was just two years old. She progressed from Dyott's "Tumble Bunnies" to elite status between ages 11 and 12, and eventually outgrew the Easton gym.
Homeschooled, she began making the trek from Denton to the Dulles Gymnastics Academy in Sterling, Virginia three times a week. She continued competing in artistic gymnastics — which includes vault, uneven bars, balance beam and floor exercise — and trampoline. But when she was 12, Raga was diagnosed with osteochondritis dissecans (OCD), a joint disorder in the elbow that can affect young gymnasts. She underwent surgery. When it was discovered the cartilage had become detached in her other elbow she again had surgery.
Despite those operations, Raga came back and qualified in the double mini for the world age group championships in Bulgaria just before her 13th birthday. Soon after, Raga's parents, Adrienne and Will Raga, conferenced with her coaches and decided instead of traveling to Virginia three times a week, Aliah would move in with a host family.
Raga shifted her focus solely to trampoline and tumbling after her elbow surgery. She continued to compete at a high level nationally and internationally, winning the USA Gymnastics championship on the double mini in 2021.
Progress was halted again in January 2023, when Raga tore three ligaments in her ankle during a practice. She avoided surgery, but was in a walking boot for weeks before going into physical therapy. Again she came back strong, winning her second national double mini title — just weeks after graduating from high school — before earning the silver medal at last year's world championships in Birmingham, England.
Raga won her third national championship in four years in Minneapolis last month.
With this being an Olympic year, there is no world championship in double mini, which is not an Olympic event. But Portugal hosted the World Cup, attracting 23 competitors from around the globe.
Then came Day 1's timing snafu.
"We didn't know they moved it up an hour," Raga said of the competition. "So when we went down there to change and get ready and warm up and stretch, (the other gymnasts) were already out on the floor getting their 15-minute warmup.
"So we had no warmup; no stretch," Raga continued. "We only took four turns before we had to salute and compete, which was honestly so stressful. Two of my teammates got injured because of it and couldn't compete their second pass because they were just so stressed."
Raga fumed, and winged her two passes in the preliminaries.
"I just took what I knew and I just did it," she said. "One of them wasn't the correct pass, but it still was enough to get me in the final in sixth place."
The top eight qualified for Sunday's Final 1 competition. And because the competition was broadcast on the Portuguese television, there would be no schedule mix-ups this time.
Each gymnast got one pass in Final 1, with the top four scores moving on to Final 2.
"When you do Final 1 and Final 2, you have to think strategically," Raga said. "Like most people will throw their harder difficulty pass first. But I know most of the girls. Their hardest difficulty is what I call my easier difficulty."
The double mini opens with a strong sprint onto the first small trampoline, where a gymnast launches upward for her first skill or aerial maneuver, lands, then launches into a second skill before a second landing.
On her Final 1 pass — which had a 7.2 degree of difficulty — Raga went through her two skills cleanly and stuck the landing for a score of 25.9, putting her in third place entering Final 2, where scores restart.
Spain's Melania Rodriguez led off Final 2. But the defending world champion, in a bid for the degree-of-difficulty record, over rotated while attempting a triple pike and rolled out on the landing. Portugal's Diana Gaga also went high risk, but couldn't complete her second skill.
Raga followed. She was again worked cleanly through her two skills. And though she took a step on her landing, her 8.4 degree of difficulty proved compensation enough to earn her a first-place mark of 26.8, giving her victory over runner-up Sienna Kuznak of Canada.
"I was nervous, but I prevailed," Raga said. "This is a really big deal for me and I'm very happy it turned out that way."

title: Board of Education's vote to resurface tennis courts leaves pickleball players feeling upended
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Board of Education's vote to resurface tennis courts leaves pickleball players feeling upended

 August 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 677
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Dozens of Cambridge's pickleball players — some with pickleball paddles in tow — left a Dorchester County Board of Education special meeting on Thursday disappointed and frustrated.Teri Eldenburg, Cambridge Pickleball Club's ambassador to USA Pickleball, said along with frustration and disappointment, she felt shock about the board's decision to approve a project by the James G. Busick Tennis Foundation to resurface the Glasgow Tennis Courts.
"It's a family, and that's going to kill that family," Eldenburg said about the project's effect on Cambridge's pickleball community.
Approval of the project means that the courts will lose the lines drawn for pickleball so only tennis can be played on the courts. This is because a grant from the United States Tennis Association, which the Busick Tennis Foundation has received, does not allow anything other than tennis lines on the courts in the first five years after they are resurfaced.
At the meeting on Thursday, Board Member Chris Wheedleton read a statement with the data points that led him to his decision on the matter. He thanked the pickleball community for their "passion and insights" on the subject.
Wheedleton said the Busick Tennis Foundation has invested more than $315,000 into the Glasgow Tennis Courts since 1992. For this upcoming project, the Busick Tennis Foundation will be contributing $219,000, resulting in a total of $444,000 contributions to the courts, he said.
"Due to this generosity, the county is able to utilize those precious dollars to use for other priorities," Wheedleton said.
Wheedleton also talked about Cambridge-South Dorchester High School's tennis team need for the courts and the potential for state tennis tournaments to be held on the courts.
The Dorchester County Recreation and Parks Department has identified 12 other pickleball courts in the county that the pickleball community can use, Wheedleton said, adding that the department is also working on a plan to build new pickleball courts. He said the department has expressed interest in building those courts on Dorchester County Public Schools property.
"I personally look forward to them bringing that plan forward, adding additional options that can help with all the parties involved," Wheedleton said.
The board unanimously voted to approve the resurfacing project. Board President Sheri Hubbard was not present.
Following the vote, many pickleball players at the meeting walked out. As they left, some residents voiced their frustrations to the board.
"Are you kidding me? We can't even comment?" one person said.
Public comment was not on the agenda for the special meeting, and so there wasn't a designated time for residents to speak. After some residents voiced concern with the lack of that opportunity, Wheedleton said people were able to and did speak at the previous board meeting on July 18.
Eldenburg, who has been playing pickleball for about four years, said in an interview that there are more than 200 people in Cambridge's pickleball community and the courts are used by pickleball players every day. She said the 12 other courts that the county has identified aren't great options because many require a fee and only allow people to play at set times.
Eldenburg, who moved to the area two years ago, said the Cambridge Pickleball Club has given her a family in Cambridge. She mentioned gatherings off the court like Christmas events and meet-ups at RaR.
"Everyone knows your name," she said.
Bill Busick with the Busick Tennis Foundation, who was also at the meeting on Thursday, said after the meeting that he understood the frustrations from the pickleball community, but said the foundation couldn't get the grant from the United States Tennis Association if they draw pickle ball lines.
Busick said the county isn't wealthy, and that is why the foundation raised its own funds to get the courts resurfaced. He said he thinks the pickleball community should organize and raise the money needed for the county to build new pickleball courts.
Eldenburg said she thinks the board's vote will have a significant affect on Cambridge's pickleball community.
"It's going to split us up," she said. "A lot of people are going to go to Easton. People aren't going to know where to play. They're going to stop playing."

title: Mautz' first goal proves to be game-winner for Saints
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Mautz' first goal proves to be game-winner for Saints

 September 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — Johnny Mautz hadn't played high school soccer before this season.Judging by the celebration he triggered midway through Tuesday night's second half, his St. Michaels High teammates are elated he decided to give the game a go this season.
Ethan Royer crossed a ball that Mautz converted into what proved to be the game-winning goal, as the Saints rallied from a halftime deficit to notch a 3-2 victory over Class 1A rival and previously unbeaten Colonel Richardson.
"I was playing baseball for awhile but I just stopped playing last year," said Mautz, a standout on the Saints' basketball team. "I never played soccer 'cause I didn't want to play three sports. But I said I might as well come out because I was only playing one sport (basketball). And then the rest is history."
There was also a touch of history attached to Mautz' score.
"That was his first goal of the year," St. Michaels head coach Pat Hambleton said of Mautz. "He's hit the post six times."
That strike with 21 minutes, 9 seconds remaining not only capped a three-goal, second-half surge, giving St. Michaels a 3-1 lead, but it also afforded the Saints (3-2 overall, 2-1 North Bayside) the breathing room they needed to weather Colonels' late-game push.
Not quite 4 minutes after having a goal erased by an offsides call, Colonel (4-1, 2-1) took a 1-0 lead on Aydan Downie's unassisted tally with 9:42 left in the first half.
St. Michaels' best chance to pull even came with just under 2 minutes to go in the first half, when Miles Fox put a shot right on Colonel keeper Cohen Carels, who made a midsection stop.
The Saints pulled even though just 1:26 into the second half, when Sherwin Mendez parked a direct kick into the back of the net for a 1-all tie.
"I think their free kick a minute and a half into the second half definitely gave them some momentum," Colonel head coach Dillon Shaheen said. "And they took that and ran with it."
Not quite 10 minutes later, Fox got deep on the left wing and steered a crossing pass that Connor Wheeler banged into the net for a 2-1 St. Michaels lead.
"Their sweeper was playing a little too far back I noticed," Hambleton said. "He was solely intercepting through balls, so I just made a small adjustment, where once he left for that through ball, I had a forward there, and it happened to be Connor. So he left, peeled off to Miles. Miles received and played that ball across, and it was wide open in the front of the net. It was just a good momentum boost that we needed to start the half."
Less than 8 minutes later, Royer slid a pass from the left side through the crease to the right post and a waiting Mautz for a 3-1 lead.
"I've been working on staying back post so that I can get whatever comes my way," Mautz said. "And Ethan played me a beautiful ball and I was just right there for the lefty finish."
Colonel wasn't quite finished though.
With 15:06 remaining, St. Michaels was called for a handball in the box. Colonel's Angel Castro Rios calmly deposited the penalty kick to the left of St. Michaels keeper Lucas Greenwood to make it a one-goal difference.
With Colonel continuing to push into the Saints' end, Hambleton dropped his team into defensive mode. St. Michaels foiled rushes and generally got in the way over the final 12 minutes, with Colonel's best chance for the equalizer coming with 6:37 left, when Greenwood smothered a loose ball near the left post in front of a charging Downie.
"Energy. They definitely came out a little more ready than we were, and we talked to them about that at halftime," Shaheen said. "I think they wanted the ball more it seemed. We match up pretty well with them, and they know they match up well with us. What it usually comes down to is which ever team plays harder, and they were definitely that team."

"I just told them we had to play harder," Kern said. "We were knocking on the doorstep the entire first half. I thought we dominated the game. We had more opportunities to score and we just couldn't get it in the net. I just told them they had to play with a little more heart."
In another physical battle that has become commonplace in this rivalry, Queen Anne's got the equalizing goal it needed, when Shannon Rath buried a penalty kick into the right side of the net in the third minute of the second half in an eventual 1-1 double-overtime tie.
While the Lions and Buccaneers each finished the regular season with identical records — 9-2-1 overall, 6-0-1 North Bayside — Queen Anne's wins the tiebreaker between the two schools based on its 1-0 victory over Kent Island on Sept. 11. Though that first meeting did not count toward the North division, it was the deciding factor since head-to-head competition is the first tiebreaker.
Queen Anne's faces two-time defending conference champion James M. Bennett (12-0) for the Bayside championship on Monday at Snow Hill High School at 6:45 p.m. It will be the fourth consecutive year the Lions and Clippers decide the conference championship. Bennett beat Queen Anne's, 3-0, on Sept. 30 in Centreville.
"I thought Olivia (Ryan) played her best game of the season," Kern said of Wednesday's clash with Kent Island. "So I think we're starting to peak a little bit. We're pretty confident. I think going against (head coach) Ed O'Leary's (Bennett) team, they know us well, we know them well. I think it's going to be a good battle.
"I think this is one of the more talented teams we've ever had," Kern continued. "I mean we can play with anybody as far from 18 to 18. We've struggled to get the ball in the back of the net against these tougher teams. But we can defend. Bennett when we played them last time, we lost 3-0, but the score didn't depict the game. We lost on the scoreboard. But we got to get the ball in the back of the net."
Queen Anne's had three direct kicks and three corner kicks in the first 17 minutes against the Bucs, but could not beat Kent Island keeper Taylor Ritz. Then with 15 minutes left in the half, Buccaneers speedster Abbie Mahaffey — with Queen Anne's Rath trying to shield her from the ball and Lions keeper Bea Holthaus moving toward the ball from the opposite direction — managed to chip a shot that floated over Holthaus for a 1-0 Kent Island lead.
"I think it was just a miscommunication," Kern said of the play. "Shannon running toward her shielding the ball, and Bea coming out. And I think Abbie just made a good play to poke a foot in there and poke it around her. It was just communication."
Kent Island, which stretched its unbeaten streak to nine games after a 1-2 start to the season, held that lead into halftime, despite the Lions swarming near the goal with less than 2 minutes left in the first half in a bid for the tying goal and Ritz away from the net. But the Bucs defense denied Queen Anne's, carrying the 1-0 lead into the break.
The Lions put immediate pressure on Kent Island early in the second half, sending a header over the crossbar. Then with almost 3 minutes elapsed, Kara Ringold was fouled just inside the box, setting up Rath, who roped a shot into the right side past Ritz's dive.
Two yellow cards against the Bucs gave Queen Anne's two more direct-kick chances, but the first sailed wide right and the second was stopped by Ritz.
The Lions came within inches of taking the lead when a shot hit under the crossbar and fell in front of the goal with 9:20 remaining in regulation.

 Giving skaters of all ages a local place to safely hone their skills, Queen Anne's County welcomed a ribbon cutting of Terrapin Skate Park in Stevensville Oct. 18.Complete with quarterpipes, ramps, rails, hubba ledges and more, Terrapin Skate Park is crafted to suit all level of skaters stands as the county's first permanent skatepark, according to Queen Anne's County Parks and Recreation Director Steve Chandlee.
Over two decades ago the parks department established a makeshift skating area but it was hidden away and not utilized well, he said.
Utilizing county owned property, an important aspect of the Terrapin Skate Park project was insuring it was in a visible location, Chandlee said.
In 2022, youths were instrumental in voicing a need to the commissioners and the Parks Advisory Board, including Kent Island High Schooler Dylan Cannon and Violet Baudean, who was a then seventh grader, created a petition highlighting the need for a skatepark.
"We knew upfront this was a great project," Chandlee said.
Now a Kent Island High School sophomore, Baudean is excited to share a love of skating with the community.
Public skateparks highlight a sense of community and offer an outlet for all ages, especially for those who don't drive, according to Baudean.
"There's something here for all skill levels, " she said.
Baudean credited county officials for their support of the project.
While skating is not a team sport, the skating community is very welcoming, always encouraging each other, Chandlee and Baudean said.
"It is a team of support for individuals," Chandlee said.
Funding for the park was made possible through a grant with the Department of Natural Resources Local Parks and Playground Infrastructure, he said.
Breaking ground in April, 12 weeks of construction opened the park to the public in June before stormwater management and tree planting completion officially welcomed the park, according to Chandlee.

The park has already become a welcome addition of the community with the hope to reach skaters far and wide.

title: Lions prepare for first state semifinal since 2004
author: Bill Haufe

Lions prepare for first state semifinal since 2004

 November 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Lexi Kern was going to get a turn regardless."The whole team knows Lexi does well with PKs," Queen Anne's County High girls head soccer coach Mike Kern said of his daughter.
Coach Kern sent his 11 players onto the field for a shootout to decide last Friday's Class 2A state quarterfinal against Wilde Lake, but noticed his third and fourth shooters had bumped themselves further back in the lineup. After Shannon Rath and Morgan Scott each buried their PKs, Kern watched his daughter move into the third spot and step behind the ball.
"She said, 'OK, I'll go,'" the coach said.
Like Rath and Scott, Lexi Kern parked her PK in the right corner, then watched Wilde Lake's third attempt miss the mark, sealing a 1-0 victory that gave the Lions their first state semifinal berth since 2004.
Second-seeded Queen Anne's (12-3-1) advances to Saturday's 2A state semifinals, where it will meet No. 3 seed Century (12-2-1) at 2:30 p.m. at Kent Island High School in Stevensville.
"That was kind of a cool moment for me," Mike Kern said of Lexi's PK. "Nobody else wanted it, which is the crazy part. Lexi is usually four or five or six (in the PK lineup). They just did not want to take it."
The Lions followed a familiar pattern against the seventh-seeded Wildecats (7-6-3), dominating play without benefit of a goal — though one score was negated by a questionable offsides call.
After two overtime periods, the game moved into penalty kicks.
"I was surprised how calm I was," said Mike Kern, who noted an eerie quiet fell over Lions Stadium during the shootout. "It was like golf. You could hear a pin drop. Both teams. After they made them they cheered. But it was quiet as could be. I had never experienced anything like that."
Queen Anne's went first, with Rath driving a shot into the right side of the net. Wilde Lake's first PK sailed over the crossbar.
Celebrating her 18th birthday, Scott deposited her PK in nearly the exact same spot at Rath's shot. The Wildecats' second attempt went wide. Lexi Kern promptly booted her shot into the right corner for a 3-0 lead. Wilde Lake's third — and final chance — again went well over the head of Lions keeper Bea Holthaus and the crossbar, clinching the victory.
This is the Lions' third trip to the state semifinals under their 24-year head coach. Queen Anne's last reached the state semis as a 1A school in 2004, when it lost in the closing minute of double overtime to Tuscarora. Queen Anne's also reached the state semifinals in 2003, outlasting Oakland Mills in an 11-man shootout before falling in the state final.
Kern and longtime assistant Jeff Anthony have built solid teams in the past, but often were eliminated by 2A powers Fallston and Bel Air.
But this season, Kern thought he had the goods to make a return trip to the final four.
"I really thought this team had the chance to get there," Kern said. "I think they're competitors. They love to compete. Even at practice with each other, they don't like to lose. And I think they accept challenges. They've been together for so long and played together for a long time. And I think they feed off each other. I think that they're competitors is the biggest thing."
Queen Anne's has posted 10 shutouts this season, and now faces a Century program that won the state title just two years ago. Since losing their first two games of the season by a combined score of 7-0, the Knights have gone 12-0-1 and logged 11 shutouts, including 10 straight.
"They very defensive," Kern said of the Knights. "They are very similar to us. I think we've got a legitimate shot."

 STEVENSVILLE — It had cut its deficit in half, rallying and grinding to a Game 3 victory.Playing on its home floor, Kent Island High's volleyball team had momentum, and may have even felt it had gained a bit of traction. But that momentum was quickly extinguished Saturday, as Williamsport built an early Game 4 lead it steadily expanded on the way to sealing a 25-16, 25-15, 23-25, 25-9 victory over the Buccaneers in a Class 2A state quarterfinal.
No. 7 Williamsport (12-5) advances to Tuesday's 2A state semifinals at Watkins Mill High School in Gaithersburg, where it will face third-seeded Calvert (15-2) at 5 p.m.
"That third set, just getting that little bit of momentum, and placing the ball and playing a little bit smarter, that's what won us the victory there," Kent Island first-year head coach Brittney Guy said.
Despite pulling within 2-1, Guy reminded her team, "That set's over with. You've got to move on. We've got to play composed and play our game."
But the Wildcats recaptured momentum early in the fourth set, getting a side out before Kennedi Lawhorne reeled off three consecutive service points for a 4-0 lead.
"We kind of got stump on our serve-receive," Williamsport head coach Karen Hampton said of the Game 3 loss. "They were serving us really tough. So once we were able to kind of fix that we kind of got back on track.
"We definitely wanted to start out with a lead," Hampton said of Game 4. "We were receiving serve, so our goal was to side out on that very first ball so we could get it and try to get the momentum early. And we were able to do that."
The second-seeded Bucs (15-3) stopped that early run via Macayla Kirk's kill to make it 4-1. An errant Kent Island return made it 8-3, bringing Skylar Norris to the service line, where she remained until delivering an ace that punctuated a 10-point service streak for an 18-3 Williamsport lead.
"Coming into the fourth set, energy was low," Guy said. "Communication was low on the court. We came back a little bit. They dug deep, but it was just a little too late in that fourth set."
Kent Island never had back-to-back service points in Game 4, as Norris' kill on the final point sealed the 25-9 victory and the Wildcats' 26th trip to the state semifinals.
"We had a bus ride; a long ride," Hampton said of her team's trip from Washington County. "So we had to kind of get loose a little bit. But once we found our groove and we found our rhythm, I felt like we were able to execute what we needed to."

The Bucs clung to their lead until a net return on a serve by Williamsport's Elizabeth Warren forged the game's first tie at 14-all. It remained tight until the Bucs struggled returning Norris' serve, helping the Wildcats score the final nine points of Game 1 for a 1-0 lead.
Game 2 was also tight early, but again Williamsport closed strong, netting the last 10 points for a 25-15 win.
"We missed a few more serves than we normally do," Guy said. "Just the technique-wise, when you come into games like this with teams like this, everything technically has to be right.
